title: Global sea surface currents on a world map

source.svs_title: Global Sea Surface Currents and Temperature
source.credit: NASA/Goddard Space Flight Center Scientific Visualization Studio
source.visualizer: Greg Shirah, Horace Mitchell, Eric Sokolowsky; scientists Hong Zhang (UCLA), Dimitris Menemenlis (NASA/JPL)
source.dataset: ECCO2 high-resolution ocean and sea ice model (MIT/NASA JPL)

frames.label: March 2007 to March 2008
frames.alt: World map of the ocean's surface currents, March 2007 to March 2008, from NASA's ECCO2 film: flow lines on dark sea around grey land, coloured by the water's temperature, blue near the poles, green and yellow in between, red in the tropics. The brightest streaks are the strong currents: the Gulf Stream off North America, the Kuroshio off Japan, the Agulhas off southern Africa, the currents along the equator, and the Southern Ocean.
frames.about: NASA's world map of the ocean's surface currents, averaged over a year. Brighter streaks are stronger currents. On the globe, the colours are the water's temperature: blue is 0 degrees Celsius, green 10 to 20, yellow about 25, red 32.

legend.summary: A slow scan line moves west to east across NASA's world map of the ocean's surface currents, March 2007 to March 2008.
legend.method: Only what is under the scan line plays. A harp note rings where the line crosses a strong current: north rings higher and in your left ear, south lower and in your right ear. A low hum follows all the moving water under the line, and is silent over land.

items.meaning: A strong current crossing the line, such as the Gulf Stream or the Kuroshio. Louder = brighter, faster water.
All the moving water under the line: quiet over calm sea, fuller over strong currents, silent over land. It is not the sound of waves.

legend.caveat: The brightness of NASA's flow lines, averaged over the year: faster water draws longer, brighter trails. Relative, not metres per second. NASA's film shows a computer model of the ocean (ECCO2). Land has no reading. The colours on the globe show temperature, which you do not hear.
